title: Principle and foundation
hook: we are made to praise, reverence and serve God; use things as far as they help

segments.voice: Yesterday, pots and pans: Brother Lawrence turning the cake for the love of God. Your line was turn it for love.

A Basque soldier is carried home with a shattered leg. Stuck in bed for a long recovery, he asks for adventure stories. The house doesn't have any. What it has is a life of Christ and a book of saints' lives. He reads them, out of boredom, and something in him turns. That's how his own Autobiography tells it. His name is Ignatius of Loyola, and you first met him on day eight hundred seventy-three. Out of what happened next came a small handbook for a guide leading someone through prayer: the Spiritual Exercises. A new room today, the Ignatian way, and it starts with one short paragraph the whole handbook stands on.

Here's the paragraph, in plain words. Human beings are created to praise, reverence and serve God our Lord, and so to save their souls. Everything else on the face of the earth is created for us, to help us toward that end. So we should use things as far as they help us toward it, and let go of them as far as they get in the way. It sounds dry, almost like an engineer wrote it. But it doesn't sort the world into holy things and bad things. Money, a job, a phone, a friendship, an ambition: none of it is the enemy, and none of it is the point. Each one gets the same quiet question: does it help? The measure is the purpose, not the thing. Paul had asked a similar question about Christian freedom: "All things are lawful unto me, but all things are not expedient." His Greek word for expedient, sympherei, means it's useful, it helps. Plenty is allowed; not all of it helps. And the opening line matters as much as the rule. Ignatius starts with what we're for: praise, reverence, service. Revelation gives that note to the elders around God's throne: "Thou art worthy, O Lord, to receive glory and honour and power: for thou hast created all things." Begin there, in Ignatius's way of seeing, and every choice gets simpler, if not always easier: not what do I want, but what helps?
screen: `USE THINGS AS FAR AS THEY HELP.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one thing that takes up real space in your life, an app, a habit, a possession, and without judging it yet, hold it up and ask: does this help me toward what I'm for? If you pray, you can ask God to show you; if you don't, ask whether it helps you love and serve well. Notice the answer, even if it's mixed.
Principle and foundation. The opening of Ignatius's Spiritual Exercises: we're made to praise, reverence and serve God, and we use everything else as far as it helps.
Your line: as far as it helps. Not good or bad, just: does it help? Until tomorrow.

howItsDone: Jesuits and others who make the Spiritual Exercises, in a long retreat or in daily life with a guide, usually begin by praying with the Principle and Foundation, and return to it when making decisions.

chat.says: Is Ignatius saying money and phones are bad, and Christians should give them up?
options: No. Nothing is the enemy or the point; you use things as far as they help you toward God.
Yes. He taught that anything enjoyable pulls the soul away and should be dropped.
No. He said all things are allowed, so whatever you enjoy must be good for you.
chat.meaning: In the principle and foundation, nothing is sorted into holy and bad. Each thing gets one question: does it help toward what we're made for?

notes: Spiritual Exercises §23 paraphrased (Mullan 1914 is pre-1929 but not on the validator's list): 'Man is created to praise, reverence and serve God our Lord, and by this means to save his soul...'. Confirm the paraphrase.
Hook: shattered leg, request for books of chivalry, a life of Christ and saints' lives in the house: from the Autobiography ch. 1. Confirm. No date or place of the battle given.
Trapdoor: 'tanto cuanto' as the Spanish phrase of §23; confirm.
Original: συμφέρει in 1 Corinthians 6:12, gloss 'it is useful, it helps'; confirm accent and pronunciation.
'Not easier, always' is a phrase about choices, not a claim about Christians.
Revelation 4:10–11 attributed to the elders around the throne; confirm.
